text: Hey, everyone.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Thanks for coming.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: I'm Andrew.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: I'm the Chief of Software at Vercel.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And I'm here to talk to you about how we solved agent building at Vercel.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: I'm the Chief of Software, so I work on a mix of internal engineering, external experimentation, and generally being at the frontier and building new libraries, frameworks, and technologies.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: For those of you that don't know Vercel, Vercel builds agentic infrastructure so people can build what's next.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: We got started in the web world, helping people ship websites and web apps without having to worry about the infrastructure that doesn't make their app any better.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: It can scale to a million and scale down to zero effortlessly.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: But we're seeing a change in what people want to build.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: You know, people started by building pages, but now we see them wanting to build agents.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And we've been embarking on a similar journey to make it easy for people to build agents and agentic applications easier.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: We built this thing called the AISCK.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So instead of needing to switch out 300, 400 lines of provider-specific code, you just need to switch out one line of code.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And we have the same model interface underlyingly for all these different providers.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: We built a lot of other tools to make it easier to have model fallbacks, secure code execution, better pricing when it's inactive and waiting for responses, as well as for durability and resumability.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And I'm here to talk to you about how I went on this crazy experiment roughly a year ago that led to an agentic explosion at Vercel and led to a really cool thing that we built recently.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: About, this is 1980, Bill Gates, before my time, had this quote saying, he imagined there would be a computer on every desk and in every home.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: You know, that was probably pretty contrarian then, and today, it seems like very normal to have that happen.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And me and the CTO had this thought, you know, instead of a computer on every desk, could we potentially have an agent on every desk?
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: You know, today we only really use agents for coding and technical workloads, but we're starting to see expansion into things like design and product management and other verticals.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And this was maybe about a year ago.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So I would say I'm pretty early to this.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: But that was when it was like Sonnet 4 and things weren't as sophisticated as they were today.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And I tried to actually explore this out, see what we could do about it.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: I went around to various job functions, Adversell, marketing, sales, finance, legal.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And I asked them, what do you hate most about your job?
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And the most compelling use case I heard was at the data team.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: They were growing, they were a very lean team, but Vercel was growing faster.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: They had so much more data from customers, analytics, metrics, sales.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: They just had to keep on aggregating and keep on making available for themselves to use.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And at this time, if you think about what the data science people ever saw to do, whenever someone from marketing or sales has a question about customer or product, the data science team has to drop everything they're doing, write the query, process it, do an analysis, and come back with some recommendation on what to do.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And this was really killer to productivity.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: You know, the data team did not want to drop everything and just write queries all day.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And so I worked with our VP of data to try to build a better way for them to operate this way.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And so if you think about the very first thing you would ever do, if you want to try to use AI to solve a problem, you may just build like a huge mega prompt.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: You know, you just have a question, you pass it into an LM, you have it respond, and that's it.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: You know, this was how the first version really looked, honestly.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: I asked them for a dump of the Snowflake schema, I pasted it into a system prompt with a question, and then when it generated SQL, I actually copy and pasted that in and just ran it myself.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: I just want to see, are the models good enough today in order to write valid SQL given some decent structure?
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And I would say this gave us a little bit of confidence that models today aren't that good, but maybe we can harness engineer or make the context around it a little better and give it some more guardrails to operate a little better.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And so if you actually think about what a data scientist actually needs to do when they get a question, they have to process the question, they may have to explore the semantic layer and actually figure out what the join patterns are.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: They will actually go and execute the SQL.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: They may go back and do that again if the SQL did not execute or if it was too expensive.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And they'll eventually report on it, including visualize the data, maybe write some paragraphs, maybe do a retro, maybe do some other stuff.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And so if you think about those different phases, me and the VP of data tried to sit down and map those out into specific agent workloads.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And so the second version of this data science agent called D0, I'm gonna reference D0 from now on, is you ask a question, we have a query agent that passes on a query to the planning agent that will then have an execution agent, et cetera.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And if you chain all of these together, you actually get something that looks like this, where each agent has a very dedicated system prompt focused to what that does with tools scoped to exactly that function.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So an example here, you can see that for the first one, the planning agent has a read entity YAML and a search schemas tool.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And so it will only use those capabilities until it has an answer to pass on to the planning agent and then to the SQL agent and then to reporting.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And this was getting better.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: We were able to get away from having to copy and paste a SQL and have to come back and report on it.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: It was now actually doing the end-to-end loop from question to answer.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: But we started hitting some walls with this architecture.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And around this time, we came to the conclusion that what you actually need is you need one agent with all the mega context within it and for it to sort of manage its own memory.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: This was around the time when
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: We realized that you want to actually have the agent be able to look back on what it's done, sort of reflect and figure out the steps I got to get here.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And with the previous model, you may have noticed that the only thing that the next agent gets is a summary and a small snippet of the previous thing that was done.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Now, this way, you can imagine that you have one mega-agent, and internally it manages its own state.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: At some points it's planning, at some points it's building, at some points it's executing, and at some points it's reporting.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And this is sort of what it looked like.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: You have one big AI call, maybe max steps 100, and you give it the ability to manage its own state based on where it's at inside of its execution journey.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And so you can see similar tools, you can see a similar shape, but the best part about this is if it ever ran into an error when executing or joining, it could go back and explore more, or it could go and read more and figure out what it was doing wrong.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And it was very good at this point.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: We were pretty confident in the actual system at hand, and we actually spread it to a few trusted members of ourself.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: You know, this was a very powerful tool, and we didn't really want to put in the hands of the wrong people or people that were using very critical workloads.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So we got into a few people's hands and the immediate response was it was awful.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: You know, we thought we were cooking.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: We thought this was, you know, nailing 30% of our evals.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: But we couldn't have anticipated some of the questions that were being asked.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And for us to spend more time manually mapping out some of these scenarios, it didn't seem like a very scalable way to do this.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And then Claude Code and Opus 4.5 came out, or more like Opus 4.5 came out, and it in tangent with Claude Code was just so powerful.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: They sort of unlocked the concept of a file system agent, and we on the side were like, wow, Claude Code and Opus 4.5 is basically AGI compared to what we had before.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: It would answer most of our questions without even missing a beat compared to the hand-grown agent we had.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And when we tried to step back and wonder what we were doing wrong and why this was so much better, we realized that the big unlock was that it was just a file system.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: It had a very minimal set of tools, list file, read file, run bash, and we gave a few more here for our own data agent use case.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: But the biggest thing was it was able to use the tools that agents are well trained on and was able to explore and write work where it needs to.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: You know, we weren't giving it, Claude Code was not giving a very prescriptive set of tools.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: It was sort of just letting it go wild and explore emergent behavior.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And so from this we learned that you can really just use a file system.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: You know, we saw the learnings from Claude Code and how powerful it was given that it just executes locally.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And we tried to rebuild it in a way that was very Claude Code-esque.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: It was now going to run in a sandbox.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: That sandbox would dump the whole semantic layer into it.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: The agent would be able to grab, bash, read file, write file, all around to figure out what it needs.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And we would just sprinkle a few tools on top to make sure it could do everything that is Vercel specific.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And this was actually the biggest unlock ever.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: The leap from single agent to Claude Code SDK, and then from Claude Code SDK to file system agent in general, fine-tuned or purpose-built for our use case, was an amazing leap.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: At this point, we were starting to get ready to give it away to more people at Vercel.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And at this point, the eval score basically doubled.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And I wrote this.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: This is basically how it looks.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: It's very simple.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: You just give it a bash tool.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: We have a nice helper called bash tool on NPM.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And you attach it to a sandbox.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And you can attach files to the sandbox for it to read, write, and execute.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And after this revelation, and after I saw that we were passing so many of the questions that we failed to do before, I wrote this banger blog post.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: It's actually up today.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And the week that I wrote this, it was responsible for 70% of our Vercel.com traffic.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So you know it's a banger.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And after that, the next logical step was that we want to figure out the common use cases we had.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So by then, we've already sort of led a leash on all of Vercel.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And we were getting thousands of queries a day from people wanting everything from customer metrics, sales metrics, number metrics, NPM downloads.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And it turns out that a lot of these queries are actually the same in shape.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: There's only so many ways you can do an aggregation, only so many ways you can look up a product, only so many ways you can do billing info.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And so we actually have a recurring job that takes the most recent queries and tries to distill them into a skill.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And right now we have roughly 100 skills that do a mix of aggregation all the way through looking up specific data about certain people.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And we found this very effective because if you think about every new agent run, it sort of just starts from nothing.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: There's really no pre-established context besides the semantic layer and the system prompts.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: But with a skill, it already starts off with a lot of contextual knowledge that has otherwise already been done.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And this is roughly how it looks.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: It's very similar to the previous one, but the inclusion of a skills folder is actually very powerful.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: We also built this tool at Vercel called SkillsSH.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: It's the most popular way to find agent skills and run them yourself.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And I'm saying all this because this journey is something that most of you may hit once in a while, where you start from something simple and you gradually add complexity and you eventually hit a system in which you can ship to prod.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And I'm telling you this because at every step along building this agent, someone Eversell was agent curious, and they tried to fork off of my D0 agent and build their own.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And at every step, we sort of had a better way to do something that was not previously known.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And we were wondering, like, what if people today could start from the very last insight and not have to ever start from just a simple prompt or from reinventing best principles from first principles?
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And so we actually thought, what if we built the Next.js for agents?
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: For those that don't know, Next.js is a popular web framework that Vercel built that invented this thing of file system framework-defined infrastructure.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: You don't have to worry about where things go.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: You just have to write files in the right conventions, and it automatically declares where they should go.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Your pages go to the CDN.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Your serverless functions go there.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Your caching goes in the middle.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And we thought building agents should be this simple.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: You should only have to create a skills folder, a tools folder, a channels folder.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And you should be able to just declare these very easily.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And the framework should know exactly how to make an agent out of it.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And that's why two weeks ago we released Eve.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Eve is an agent framework like the Next.js for agents where it's very easy from just starting with a sample template to having a fully agent ready and being able to add in your own custom knowledge, your own custom tools, and even integrate it into the channels that you are familiar with.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: This is roughly what we think an agent actually looks like.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: You know, an agent has a runtime and it has channels.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And in that runtime, you're going to have durability.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: You're going to want to run things in an isolated environment.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: You're going to want to call into different models.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And you're going to want to have connections.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And we built this with open source in mind.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: We built Eve so you can plug in your own open source adapters for Postgres, OpenAI's response API, Docker, other connectors.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: But we also made it incredibly easy to deploy on Vercel.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: The only thing here you see different is that everything here is using a Vercel product that we've been building over the years in order to make it easy to build these experiences.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Vercel workflows for durability, Sandbox for secure execution, and Vercel Connect, something we just released to make it easy to generate short-lived OIDC tokens for connections.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And we actually rewrote the whole D0 agent in Eve as we were building Eve.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And from the convoluted structures behind the scenes that you did not see from the code, this is roughly how the file system looks.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: It's very simple.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: You have a bunch of system instructions, a couple skills, a couple tools, and it's very easy to compose this into a real agent.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And it's very easy to iterate on.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: We actually gave this out to a few beta customers before we actually fully released it two weeks ago at our London event.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And this one company that partners closely with us, Aura, they've rebuilt their agent that's sort of like a mini claw to go and test people's services.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: It goes to websites, installs them, it tries to use them.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And they've seen incredible success on building their own agent from the ground up using Eve compared to using an off-the-shelf Claude Code.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Fewer steps, better successes, as well as better insights.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And when you deploy Eve to Vercel, you get observability out of the box.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: You can see here that you get all the agent runs, you see all the tool calls, you see each step it takes, as well as maybe some estimated costs and some optimizations you could potentially take.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And you can start today at eve.dev.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: You can just clone it, and you can just start a template, deploy easily, self-host if you need.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And the reason why I bring this up is because I hope that there will be more and more business-specific use case agents.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: You know, before we built EZero, we actually battle-tested a lot of the industry, well-funded startups that were doing these vertical agents that were dedicated to taking your Snowflake instance
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And making it so their agent could run Snowflake queries against it.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: But we found out that what really makes this agent good is it has a lot of very specific company knowledge.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: You know, the way that Vercel is a web-based company, we have a lot of customers that have websites and web properties.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: That goes a lot deeper into when you should query for what and what things link to what.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And so a lot of these off-the-shelf agents, they're great, they're good to try, but I think if you really want to get the most juice out of a squeeze, you should really try to build your own agent and add in as much company-specific knowledge as you can.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Today, you know, we've had 20 roughly decently PMF agents ever sell.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: That range from anything from marketing retros to figure out who to reach out to, to the first ever red line of a contract when legal sees a new negotiation, all the way to my data science agents helping with data queries.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And that goes to show that we at Vercel have been very agent-pilled.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: The data team has never been more productive.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: They have more time to go and improve the performance of Snowflake, to add new data sources that were missing, to fill in the gaps that they previously did not have time to because they were so busy writing queries.
speaker: SPEAKER_00
